# Adaptive cap multiplicity: an attained capacity bound

This is a proved instance of the adaptive pairing mechanism. It applies
to a planar simplex middle fiber and a left fiber that is a translated
positive homothet of that simplex. The right fiber can be any convex body.
No universal target density or common coupling for all possible cap
families is asserted.

Let `K` be a planar simplex of area `k>0`, with barycentric coordinates
`lambda_0,lambda_1,lambda_2`. Define its three closed centroid facet caps
and their multiplicity by

    C_i={x in K:lambda_i(x)>=1/3},
    N(x)=sum_{i=0}^2 1_{C_i}(x),
    D={x in K:N(x)>=2}.

The three caps cover `K`. Their individual areas are `4k/9`. Their
pairwise overlaps are three triangles of area `k/9`, meeting only at
the centroid, so `|D|=k/3`. Away from the centroid, `N=1+1_D`.

## 1. A degree bound for sufficiently large homothetic subtriangles

If `Q=t+sigma K subset K` is a translated positive homothet with
`sigma>=1/2`, then

    |Q intersect D|>=2|Q|/9.                       (1)

To prove this, parameterize a uniform point of `Q` by a uniform point
`X` in `K`. Its barycentric coordinates have the form

    lambda_i(t+sigma X)=l_i+sigma lambda_i(X),
    l_i>=0, sum_i l_i=1-sigma.

The containment `Q subset K` gives `l_i>=0` by evaluating at the two
vertices where `lambda_i=0`. It also gives `sigma<=1`. Set

    s_i=(1/3-l_i)/sigma.

Then

    sum_i s_i=1, -1/3<=s_i<=2/3.                  (2)

The upper bound follows from `l_i>=0` and `sigma>=1/2`. For the lower
bound use `l_i<=1-sigma`, giving
`s_i>=1-2/(3sigma)>=-1/3`.

If all `s_i>=0`, the conditional cap probabilities on `Q` are
`(1-s_i)^2`. Their sum is at least `4/3` by the elementary inequality
`sum(1-s_i)^2>=3[(sum(1-s_i))/3]^2=4/3`. Because the triple overlap is
at most a point, `|Q intersect D|/|Q|` equals this sum minus one and is
at least `1/3`.

Otherwise exactly one threshold, say `s_0`, is negative. There cannot
be two: (2) would make the remaining threshold exceed one, contrary to
its upper bound. Cap zero now contains all of `Q`. The other two caps
are disjoint up to null boundaries, since `s_1+s_2=1-s_0>1`. Hence

    |Q intersect D|/|Q|
      =(1-s_1)^2+(1-s_2)^2
      >=(1+s_0)^2/2>=2/9.

This proves (1), including the zero-threshold cases by either direct
evaluation or the first case. Equality is attained at a scale-one-half
subtriangle based at a vertex of `K`.

## 2. A compact capacity-matching lemma with attainment

Let `A,B` be compact sets with finite positive Lebesgue measures `a,b`,
and let `G subset A x B` be closed. Suppose there is `c>0` such that

    |{x in A:(x,y) in G}|>=c for every y in B.      (3)

There exists a nonnegative measure `pi` supported on `G`, with both
marginals dominated respectively by `1_A dx` and `1_B dy`, of mass

    |pi|>=min(b,c).                               (4)

Moreover a maximum-mass such measure is attained. Indeed these measures
form a nonempty compact set for weak convergence: their support is in
the compact product, total mass is uniformly bounded, marginal
domination is closed under testing against nonnegative continuous
functions, and support in the closed set `G` is preserved under weak
limits. The mass functional is continuous, so take a maximizer of mass
`g`.

Suppose `g<min(b,c)`. Let

    alpha=1_A dx-pi_A, beta=1_B dy-pi_B

be its residual capacity measures. For every `y in B`,

    alpha(G_y)>=c-g>0,

because the used first marginal has total mass only `g`. Thus the
restriction `eta=1_G(alpha x beta)` has mass at least
`(c-g)(b-g)>0`. Its marginals satisfy

    eta_A<=(b-g)alpha, eta_B<=(a-g)beta.

A sufficiently small positive multiple of `eta` can therefore be added
to `pi` without violating either capacity, contradicting maximality.
This proves (4). The argument is a direct continuous capacity
augmentation proof; it does not assume a matching exists.

If `a>=b`, this partial matching can always be completed to a coupling
of all of `1_B dy` and a left submeasure bounded by `1_A dx`. If `g<b`,
use the residual right measure `beta` and the left submeasure

    rho_A=[(b-g)/(a-g)]alpha.

Their masses both equal `b-g`; their normalized product is a coupling
of them. Add it to `pi`. If `g=b`, no completion is necessary.

## 3. Balanced three-fiber multiplicity bound

Let `A,K,B` be consecutive continuous fibers of a convex mixed set at
integer coordinates `-1,0,1`. It suffices to assume directly that

    (A+B)/2 subset K.

Suppose `A` is a translated positive homothet of the planar simplex
`K`, while `B` is any compact convex planar body. Write their areas as
`a,k,b`, and assume

    a=k+b, b>0.                                   (5)

For every `y in B`, the set `Q_y=(A+y)/2` is a homothetic subtriangle of
`K` of scale `sqrt(a/k)/2>=1/2`. Applying (1) and undoing its area
dilation gives

    |{x in A:(x+y)/2 in D}|
      =4|Q_y intersect D|>=2a/9.                 (6)

The relation `G={(x,y):(x+y)/2 in D}` is closed in the compact product.
The capacity lemma supplies a good partial pairing of mass at least
`min(b,2a/9)`, and its completion uses all of `B` and at most unit
Lebesgue density in `A`. Every pair output belongs to `K` and therefore
has `N>=1`; outputs from the good matching have `N>=2`. Thus for this
completed coupling `Pi`,

    int N((x+y)/2) dPi(x,y)
      >=b+min(b,2a/9).                            (7)

Brunn-Minkowski and (5) give the useful exact ratio bound

    2 sqrt(k)>=sqrt(a)+sqrt(b), b/a<=9/25.         (8)

For the last implication set `r=sqrt(b/a)` and use `k/a=1-r^2`:
`2sqrt(1-r^2)>=1+r`, whence `5r^2+2r-3<=0` and `r<=3/5`.
In particular `2a/9>b/3`, and also `b>b/3`; hence (7) is strictly
larger than `4b/3`.

The supremum of this multiplicity objective over all completed couplings
is attained as well. The admissible couplings have fixed mass `b` and
form a compact set under weak convergence, while the bounded function
`N((x+y)/2)` is upper semicontinuous as a sum of indicators of closed
sets. The weak-limit upper-bound inequality for such functions gives
an attained maximum. The proved estimate (7) does not require its exact
value.

## 4. Consequence for ambient caps with the three prescribed middle traces

Let `H_0,H_1,H_2` be any three closed ambient halfspaces whose traces on
the middle fiber are precisely the three centroid facet caps above.
Their integer coefficients can be arbitrary, so oblique caps are fully
included. The affine midpoint identity gives pointwise

    1_{H_i}(0,(x+y)/2)
      <=1_{H_i}(-1,x)+1_{H_i}(1,y).

Integrate against the completed coupling. Its left marginal is bounded
by the left fiber volume and its right marginal equals the whole right
fiber volume. Add the three disjoint middle-fiber contributions to get

    sum_{i=0}^2 mu(H_i)
      >=4k/3+int N((x+y)/2)dPi
      >4(k+b)/3=3 gamma_2 a.                      (9)

Consequently these three ambient caps cannot all have total mass below
`gamma_2 a`. This establishes the proposed adaptive finite-cover
contradiction for this stated geometric subclass, using a coupling
adapted to the three caps and no regularized target law.

If `b=0`, then `a=k`; each of the prescribed middle traces already has
mass `gamma_2 k=gamma_2 a`, so the same impossibility of three strictly
smaller caps follows without pairing. The positive-body assumptions
above avoid other zero-area issues.

## Scope

The homothety of `A` to `K` is a genuine hypothesis in (6). For an
arbitrary convex `A`, its translated halves are arbitrary convex subsets
of `K`, so Lemma 1 does not apply. No classification of such subsets is
being assumed, and this note does not prove a general three-fiber
theorem, a sharp middle-fiber lifting theorem, or OC.

The constants and the finite-dimensional inequality in the homothetic
lemma are checked by `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_adaptive_cap_multiplicity.py`; the compact
matching existence and augmentation argument are proved above.
